mwg:install-web-app.title: Use <install> / navigator.install() instead of beforeinstallprompt, which can only install itself
mwg:install-web-app.action: Offer an explicit in-page install entry with the HTML `<install>` element or `navigator.install()`, including installing *other* apps (for example from an app catalog)
mwg:install-web-app.blocker: The existing `beforeinstallprompt` can only install the current app; a catalog cannot offer installs for other apps (quote: "Unlike `navigator.install()`, this event cannot install a different app.")
mwg:install-web-app.outcome: Neither new entry point is supported by any major browser yet; in practice you still rely on `beforeinstallprompt` or the browser's own install UI (official claim)
mwg:install-web-app.story: The guide funnels installation through browser-controlled consent UI, so sites cannot install silently. The new entry points would let a catalog install other apps in one click, but the guide states "<install> is not natively supported by any major browser yet", and the same goes for `navigator.install()`. Until support lands, the only fallback is the old event, which is exactly what cannot install across apps.
mwg:install-web-app.unlock: One page could offer install buttons for *other* web apps, so a self-made catalog or toolbox page could install each small tool in one click. No browser supports it yet; track it for now.
mwg:install-web-app.support: `<install>`: not natively supported by any major browser yet; `navigator.install()`: same; Web app manifest: Limited (not in Firefox)

mwg:single-line-overflow.title: Truncate visually with CSS instead of cutting strings in script
mwg:single-line-overflow.action: When a single-line label (tab, table cell, file name) is too long, truncate only on screen with `text-overflow: ellipsis` or a mask fade, keeping the full text in the DOM
mwg:single-line-overflow.blocker: Cutting the string in script means screen readers, find-in-page and copy all get the mangled text (quote: "Screen readers announce the full text, find-in-page matches it, and copying copies it. This is why the string must never be cut in script.")
mwg:single-line-overflow.outcome: Truncation happens only at paint time; assistive tech, search and copy still get the full text. Ellipsis and masks are Widely available (official claim)
mwg:single-line-overflow.story: The common approach is to cut the string to N characters before rendering and append "…", which removes the full text from the DOM. The guide requires truncation to be visual only; to keep a tail such as a file extension, split it in the markup rather than cutting characters. Another trap: a single gradient mask also hides the focus outline ("it also hides the element's focus outline").

mwg:single-line-overflow:2.title: Make truncated text reachable for keyboard and touch too
mwg:single-line-overflow:2.action: Scroll the text into view on `:hover` and `:focus-visible`, with scroll-driven animations controlling the fade and hint
mwg:single-line-overflow:2.blocker: Relying on the `title` attribute alone to show the full text leaves keyboard and touch users without it (quote: "DO NOT rely on `title` alone: it is unreachable from the keyboard and on touch.")
mwg:single-line-overflow:2.outcome: Keyboard users see the full text via focus, but touch still has no hover or focus, so the guide asks for another route (the selected item is never truncated, a detail view opens). Scroll-driven animations only just became Newly available (official claim)
mwg:single-line-overflow:2.story: `title` is the easiest option but only works with a mouse. The new approach scrolls the text inside its box on hover and focus, shrinking the fade as it scrolls so the end is readable. The guide also admits "Hover and focus reveal nothing on touch", so on touch the opponent is sidestepped by interface design rather than defeated by the feature. Without scroll-driven animations, the fade and hint never appear and the text is clipped with no indication; a `ResizeObserver` fallback is needed.
mwg:single-line-overflow:2.unlock: Truncated long labels (file names, tab names) can scroll to reveal the full text on hover or focus in pure CSS, with no JS width measuring and no `title`.
mwg:single-line-overflow:2.support: Scroll-driven animations: Newly (2026-10-27); Container style queries: Newly (2026-05-19)

mwg:drag-and-drop.title: Move the real DOM nodes instead of faking order with CSS
mwg:drag-and-drop.action: On drop, move the existing node once with `container.moveBefore(item, ref)` so visual, keyboard and reading order stay aligned
mwg:drag-and-drop.blocker: Changing on-screen order with CSS `order` or `flex-direction: *-reverse` leaves DOM order unchanged, so Tab and screen readers follow the old order (quote: "Reorder the real children in the DOM (not via CSS `order` or `flex-direction: *-reverse`) so visual, keyboard, and reading order stay aligned.")
mwg:drag-and-drop.outcome: Moving real nodes fixes the order mismatch, but keeping internal state needs `moveBefore()`, which Safari lacks; the `before()` fallback loses focus and other state inside items (official claim)
mwg:drag-and-drop.story: The cheapest drag-to-reorder is changing `order`: it looks right, but keyboard users jump through the old order. The guide moves the real node once on release and uses `moveBefore()` to keep focus and iframe state. When visual and DOM order truly cannot match in a complex layout, `reading-flow` is the tool, but only Chrome/Edge support it.
mwg:drag-and-drop.unlock: A playing video, a live iframe widget or a half-filled form can be moved elsewhere without resetting. Previously every move reloaded it, which made a rearrangeable live dashboard painful.
mwg:drag-and-drop.support: moveBefore(): Limited (Chrome 133, Edge 133, Firefox 144; not Safari); reading-flow: Limited (Chrome/Edge 137; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:drag-and-drop:2.title: Show a drop marker while dragging; move only on release
mwg:drag-and-drop:2.action: Keep the source item in its slot during the drag, draw a drop marker with `::before`/`::after`, and move on `pointerup`
mwg:drag-and-drop:2.blocker: Reordering live while dragging makes siblings shift and the list jitter (quote: "Don't reorder while the pointer moves: shifting siblings feel jittery.")
mwg:drag-and-drop:2.outcome: A drop marker replaces live shifting and the jitter is gone; pointer capture and fixed positioning are mature features (official claim)
mwg:drag-and-drop:2.story: Many drag implementations reorder on `pointermove`, so the whole list jumps every time the pointer passes an item. The guide shows only a drop line during the drag, moves once on release, and animates every move so items travel instead of jumping.

mwg:dynamic-sort.title: Sort by moving existing nodes, not rebuilding with innerHTML
mwg:dynamic-sort.action: When the user changes sort order, move the existing nodes into the new order with `moveBefore()`, optionally wrapped in a view transition
mwg:dynamic-sort.blocker: Creating new nodes with `innerHTML` or a full re-render loses focus, scroll position inside items and image state, and breaks view transitions (quote: "Recreating nodes with `innerHTML` or a re-render that replaces them discards focus, scroll position inside items, and image state, and it breaks view transitions, which match old and new elements by identity.")
mwg:dynamic-sort.outcome: Moving nodes alone stops focus and scroll loss. `moveBefore()` is missing in Safari; the `append()` fallback keeps order but may lose iframe, animation or inner focus state. View transitions are Newly (official claim)
mwg:dynamic-sort.story: Redrawing the whole list after sorting is the usual approach, and the cost is that the button the user just clicked loses focus and a half-scrolled card jumps to the top. The guide turns sorting into "moving house" rather than "rebuilding", with animation as an optional enhancement.
mwg:dynamic-sort.unlock: After sorting or filtering, the list animates items to their new places with a view transition while scroll, focus and playback inside each item survive. Suits lists of heavy items (embedded previews, video cards).
mwg:dynamic-sort.support: moveBefore(): Limited (not Safari); View transitions: Newly (2025-10-14)

mwg:dynamic-sort:2.title: Announce the sort result once
mwg:dynamic-sort:2.action: Announce the result once through a single `role="status"` region and keep focus on the control that triggered the sort
mwg:dynamic-sort:2.blocker: Putting `aria-live` on the list makes every moved item get announced (quote: "DO NOT put `aria-live` on the list, which would announce every moved item.")
mwg:dynamic-sort:2.outcome: The user performed one action and hears one announcement (official claim)
mwg:dynamic-sort:2.story: A reorder moves many nodes, but the user did one thing. With `aria-live` on the list, screen readers treat every node move as an update. A single status region announcing once is enough.

mwg:sortable-table.title: Move <tr> elements when sorting; don't rebuild the tbody
mwg:sortable-table.action: When a `<button>` in a column header is clicked, move the existing `<tr>` elements within `<tbody>` and mark the sorted column with `aria-sort`
mwg:sortable-table.blocker: Rebuilding `<tbody>` with `innerHTML` or a re-render on sort loses focus and row state and breaks view transitions (quote: "DO NOT re-render the `<tbody>` or `<table>` on sort; it discards focus and state and breaks view transitions.")
mwg:sortable-table.outcome: Moving existing rows uses mature DOM operations and focus stays on the header button; animation is optional (official claim)
mwg:sortable-table.story: This is the table version of dynamic-sort. The guide also puts the button inside `<th>` rather than making `<th>` clickable, keeps `aria-sort` on one column only, and keeps the button label as the column name instead of "Sort ascending". Invoker commands are recommended over a click listener per button, but without saying what concretely goes wrong with the old way.

mwg:sortable-table:2.title: Compare by column type, not formatted strings
mwg:sortable-table:2.action: Declare each column's type with `data-type` and compare numbers and dates by their underlying values
mwg:sortable-table:2.blocker: Comparing the formatted strings on screen sorts numbers and dates in the wrong order (quote: "DO NOT sort formatted strings when the underlying values are numbers or dates.")
mwg:sortable-table:2.outcome: Type-aware comparison gives the correct order; no new feature involved (official claim)
mwg:sortable-table:2.story: "1,200" sorting before "950", or "2026/1/10" before "2025/12/3", is what string comparison does. The guide has each column declare its type instead of guessing from content.

mwg:accordion.title: Don't put headings inside summary when items need their own heading
mwg:accordion.action: Build accordions from adjacent `<details>`; when each item needs its own heading, build a custom accordion instead
mwg:accordion.blocker: With a heading inside `<summary>`, JAWS and TalkBack expose summary as a button and drop the heading, so users cannot jump between items by heading (quote: "JAWS and TalkBack expose `summary` as a button and drop any heading inside it, so their users cannot move between items by heading.")
mwg:accordion.outcome: A custom accordion keeps the headings in the accessibility tree (official claim)
mwg:accordion.story: `<details>` makes a good accordion, but the summary role swallows inner structure. The guide names two specific screen readers, which makes this an opponent you can verify yourself. The navbar guide gives the same warning about inconsistent summary roles.

mwg:accordion:2.title: Avoid exclusive <details name> so content doesn't jump out of view
mwg:accordion:2.action: Allow several items open at once by default; don't use the exclusive behaviour of `<details name>`
mwg:accordion:2.blocker: In an exclusive accordion, opening one item closes another and content shifts out of view, which seriously affects screen-magnifier users (quote: "They also can cause content to shift out of the user’s view which can cause significant problems for those using screen magnifiers.")
mwg:accordion:2.outcome: Without exclusivity there is no such shift; the guide takes a clear stance where the new feature itself is the opponent (official claim)
mwg:accordion:2.story: `<details name>` only became Baseline in 2024, yet the guide advises against it. What makes this line unusual is that the opponent is not an old technique but a side effect of a new feature. When exclusivity is truly needed, the guide says to use it only as a last resort.

mwg:accordion:3.title: Collapse with ::details-content to keep find-in-page and animation
mwg:accordion:3.action: Collapsed content lives in `::details-content` and is hidden with `content-visibility: hidden` rather than `display: none`
mwg:accordion:3.blocker: Hiding collapsed content with `display: none` makes it unfindable by find-in-page and its height cannot animate (quote: "While closed it is hidden with `content-visibility: hidden`, not `display: none`, which is what keeps it findable and lets its size animate.")
mwg:accordion:3.outcome: In supporting browsers content is searchable and slides open; `::details-content` is only Newly, so older browsers get no animation (official claim)
mwg:accordion:3.story: Once a collapsed section is `display: none`, Ctrl+F cannot find it. A closed `<details>` hides its content with `content-visibility: hidden` instead, so the content is still there and searchable, and the browser opens it automatically on a search hit. The `::details-content` pseudo-element is what lets you select, style and animate the height of the collapsed part. Conversely, use `display: none` deliberately when the content should not be searchable.
mwg:accordion:3.unlock: A long page can be fully collapsed while Ctrl+F still finds and expands matches, with an opening animation. Long docs, FAQs and weekly notes no longer have to choose between collapsing and being findable.
mwg:accordion:3.support: `<details>` auto-opens on find-in-page match: Chrome 97, Firefox 148, Safari 26.2 (Safari does not scroll to the matched text correctly, WebKit bug 304174; not mapped to any web-features feature, so no Baseline label); ::details-content: Newly (2025-09-16); transition-behavior: Newly (2024-08-06)

mwg:app-menus.title: Pin menus to their trigger with anchor positioning
mwg:app-menus.action: Each menu in a menu bar (File/Edit/View) is a popover placed next to its trigger with CSS anchor positioning
mwg:app-menus.blocker: Without anchor positioning a popover falls back to the centered viewport position, detaching the menu from its trigger, and a centered submenu covers its parent (quote: "Never ship that for a menu: it detaches the menu from its trigger, and a centered submenu covers its parent.")
mwg:app-menus.outcome: Menus stay attached to their triggers. The core anchor properties (`anchor-name`, `position-area`, `anchor()`) are supported in Chrome 125, Firefox 147 and Safari 26 (Baseline Newly, 2026-01-13); older browsers still need an `@supports` gate (official claim; support corrected after verification on 2026-11-12)
mwg:app-menus.story: A menu bar is one widget: one Tab stop, left/right arrows switch menus, focus previews. Each menu must sit under its trigger, but a native popover defaults to the middle of the viewport. The guide's support section says anchor positioning is "supported only in Safari 27", but that is the status of the whole feature group, not of the properties this guide uses; see the details.
mwg:app-menus.unlock: A desktop-style File/Edit/View menu bar can be built almost declaratively with popover plus anchor positioning, with menus attached to their buttons. Web tools can look and behave like desktop programs.
mwg:app-menus.support: Anchor positioning core properties: Newly (2026-01-13; `position-anchor` 2026-09-14). The guide says "Supported by: Safari 27. Unsupported in: Chrome, Edge, and Firefox.", which is the lowest common support of the whole web-features `anchor-positioning` group (325 sub-features); Chrome and Firefox only lack the `position-visibility: anchor-valid / anchor-visible` values (Chrome 157 beta, not Firefox), which this guide does not use. Popover: Newly (2025-01-27); focusgroup: Limited (Chrome/Edge 150)

mwg:breadcrumbs.title: Keep separators so breadcrumbs read as a hierarchy, not siblings
mwg:breadcrumbs.action: Build breadcrumbs with `<nav>` + `<ol>`, with separators generated in CSS and hidden from assistive tech
mwg:breadcrumbs.blocker: Pill or segmented styles without separators look like tabs or filters (items on the same level), not a hierarchy (quote: "Pills, tags and a segmented bar without one look like tabs or filters (items on the same level), not a hierarchy.")
mwg:breadcrumbs.outcome: Separators are CSS-generated content and work in every browser (official claim)
mwg:breadcrumbs.story: Designers often want breadcrumbs to look more like a button row, and the result implies the wrong structure. The guide treats separators as essential and uses `ol` rather than `ul` to express order.

mwg:breadcrumbs:2.title: Use border-shape so borders and focus rings follow slanted segments
mwg:breadcrumbs:2.action: Draw slanted or arrow-shaped segments with `corner-shape` / `border-shape`, with borders and focus outlines following the shape
mwg:breadcrumbs:2.blocker: Cutting shapes with `clip-path` also clips borders and focus outlines; forced-colors mode removes the background, so a clipped segment loses its outline (quote: "`clip-path` clips borders and outlines, so under the fallback use a color/background change plus negative `outline-offset` for focus instead of an outside outline.")
mwg:breadcrumbs:2.outcome: `corner-shape` and `border-shape` are Chrome/Edge only; other browsers fall back to rectangular segments with separators, and the guide says rounded corners are not an acceptable substitute for slants (official claim)
mwg:breadcrumbs:2.story: Arrow-shaped breadcrumbs used to rely on `clip-path`, so the keyboard focus ring was cut off and whole segments vanished in high-contrast mode. The new properties make the border itself the shape, but Firefox and Safari do not support them yet.
mwg:breadcrumbs:2.unlock: Slanted, arrow or notched shapes can carry their borders and focus rings along the shape, without sacrificing accessibility to clip-path. Chromium only for now.

mwg:carousel.title: Loop a carousel without cloning slides by parking one with order
mwg:carousel.action: For looping, use `--current` and CSS `order` to park the first or last slide beside the current one and mark it `inert`, without cloning or moving slides
mwg:carousel.blocker: Cloning slides or moving them in the DOM for infinite looping conflicts with frameworks and makes assistive tech read duplicate content (quote: "Do not clone slides or move them in the DOM, which conflicts with frameworks and duplicates content for assistive technology.")
mwg:carousel.outcome: No clones means no duplicate content, but the offset must be compensated when scrolling settles with snapping briefly turned off, and `scrollend` is only Newly (official claim)
mwg:carousel.story: The usual infinite carousel clones a slide at each end, so screen readers hear the same slide twice. The guide instead visually parks a single slide at the other end and makes it inert, so Tab order and the accessibility tree match what is on screen. The guide also says not to use `::scroll-button()` / `::scroll-marker` "for now", without giving a reason.
mwg:carousel.unlock: An infinitely looping carousel without cloned slides: park one slide with CSS order and compensate the offset once scrolling settles. Content exists once, so frameworks and screen readers don't fight.
mwg:carousel.support: Scroll snap: Widely (2020-01-15); scrollend: Newly (2025-12-12); Scroll-driven animations: Newly (2026-10-27)

mwg:copy-button.title: Don't disable the button while showing feedback
mwg:copy-button.action: After copying, show feedback; on repeat clicks, reset the timer and restart the animation instead of setting the button to disabled
mwg:copy-button.blocker: Disabling the button during feedback drops keyboard focus and announces a misleading unavailable state (quote: "DO NOT disable the button while showing feedback: copying is idempotent, and disabling drops keyboard focus, announces a misleading unavailable state")
mwg:copy-button.outcome: The button stays usable and focus stays put (official claim)
mwg:copy-button.story: Disabling the button to prevent double clicks is an intuitive safeguard, but copying twice has no side effect. Disabling makes a keyboard user's next Tab start again from the top of the page.

mwg:copy-button:2.title: Declare the copy target with Invoker Commands
mwg:copy-button:2.action: Use `command` + `commandfor` to declare which element a button copies, instead of wiring JavaScript to each button
mwg:copy-button:2.blocker: (missing) The guide only says it replaces "per-button JavaScript wiring" without pointing to a moment where the old way fails (quote: "Declare the target with Invoker Commands (`command` + `commandfor`) instead of per-button JavaScript wiring")
mwg:copy-button:2.outcome: The guide does not say what improves with invoker commands; the fallback when unsupported is "add a click listener that calls the same function", i.e. the old way (official claim)
mwg:copy-button:2.story: The same recommendation appears in sortable-table and accordion: declarative attributes instead of click listeners. None of the three guides says where hand-wired listeners break; they only describe the new style. Both slot 3 and the outcome are missing on this line.
mwg:copy-button:2.unlock: What a button does to another element can be written directly in HTML (`command`/`commandfor`) with no JS wiring; custom `--commands` let one button trigger any behaviour.

mwg:copy-button:3.title: Hide repeated copy buttons with opacity
mwg:copy-button:3.action: Hide the many repeated copy buttons on a page until hover or focus, using only `opacity`
mwg:copy-button:3.blocker: Hiding buttons with `display: none` or `visibility: hidden` removes them from the tab order, so keyboard users can never reach them (quote: "`display: none` and `visibility: hidden` remove the button from the tab order, so keyboard users could never reach it.")
mwg:copy-button:3.outcome: Opacity hiding does not affect focusability; devices without hover always show the button (official claim)
mwg:copy-button:3.story: A copy button on every code block is noisy, so they are often shown only on hover. The catch is how they are hidden: most hiding methods also take the button out of the Tab order. The guide also forbids "hiding" with `aria-hidden` or `inert`.

mwg:navbar.title: No hard-coded breakpoint: collapse only when it doesn't fit
mwg:navbar.action: Use one `<nav>` tree; script compares `scrollWidth` with `clientWidth` and collapses into a native popover only when the row doesn't fit
mwg:navbar.blocker: With a hard-coded breakpoint, adding a link, switching language or enlarging text makes the nav overflow or collapse too early at the wrong width (quote: "There is no hard-coded breakpoint. Script collapses the navigation only when the inline row (brand, actions and every link) does not fit, so adding a link, a translation or larger text moves the point automatically.")
mwg:navbar.outcome: The collapse point follows the actual content, but deciding still needs JS measurement; popover is Newly and older browsers need a polyfill (official claim)
mwg:navbar.story: Traditional navbars switch to a hamburger at a fixed media-query width, so after translation into a longer language the links overflow before the breakpoint. The guide measures whether the row actually fits, and defaults to the collapsed layout without script so it always works.
mwg:navbar.unlock: A navbar collapses into a native popover when it doesn't fit, with keyboard, Esc and click-outside closing built in; changing the number of links or the language needs no breakpoint tuning.

mwg:navbar:2.title: Use button + aria-expanded for submenus, not details/summary
mwg:navbar:2.action: Trigger nested navigation with `<button aria-expanded aria-controls>`, immediately followed by the submenu list
mwg:navbar:2.blocker: Building submenus with `<details>`/`<summary>`: `summary` should map to the button role but is not implemented consistently (quote: "DO NOT use `<details>` and `<summary>`: `<summary>` should map to a `button` role, but has not been consistently implemented")
mwg:navbar:2.outcome: The button role is consistent across assistive tech (official claim)
mwg:navbar:2.story: Same opponent as the accordion guide: summary behaves differently across screen readers. `<details>` opens and closes without JS, which is tempting, but in navigation an unstable role costs more.

mwg:tabs.title: Replace hand-written roving tabindex with focusgroup
mwg:tabs.action: Put `focusgroup` on the tablist to get the right roles and arrow-key movement automatically
mwg:tabs.blocker: (missing) The guide only says it replaces manually implementing roving tabindex or activedescendant, without saying where the hand-written version fails (quote: "Instead of manually implementing a roving tabindex or ARIA activedescendant pattern to meet the focus management requirement of the ARIA `tablist` role, we can use `focusgroup`")
mwg:tabs.outcome: `focusgroup` is only in Chrome/Edge 150; Firefox and Safari still need the hand-written version (official claim)
mwg:tabs.story: The tabs keyboard model (one Tab stop, arrows switch) has always been hand-written. The new attribute lets the browser do it, but the opponent is described only as "implementing it manually": effort, not an observable failure.
mwg:tabs.unlock: "One Tab stop, arrows move inside" for a group of elements becomes a single attribute instead of hand-written roving tabindex. Keyboard-first interfaces (grid menus, kanban boards) get much cheaper; Chromium only for now.
mwg:tabs.support: focusgroup: Limited (Chrome/Edge 150; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:tabs:2.title: Draw the selected underline as a pseudo-element border so it survives forced colors
mwg:tabs:2.action: Draw the selected tab's underline with a border on a pseudo-element, styled from `aria-selected`
mwg:tabs:2.blocker: Drawing the underline with `box-shadow` or a background leaves no indicator at all, because forced-colors mode removes both (quote: "DO NOT use `box-shadow` or a background: forced colors mode removes both, leaving no indicator.")
mwg:tabs:2.outcome: Borders survive forced-colors mode, so the selected state stays visible (official claim)
mwg:tabs:2.story: High-contrast users otherwise see a row of identical buttons. The guide also forbids indicating selection with colour alone (WCAG 1.4.1) and ties styling to `aria-selected`, so the visual and accessible states cannot disagree.

mwg:tabs:3.title: Keep tabs on one row; scroll or overflow into a menu
mwg:tabs:3.action: Keep tabs on a single row; when they don't fit, scroll horizontally with edge fades or move extras into a "More" menu
mwg:tabs:3.blocker: Wrapping tabs onto several rows makes the tab order and the selected tab hard to follow (quote: "DO NOT wrap them onto multiple rows: wrapped rows make the tab order and the selected tab hard to follow.")
mwg:tabs:3.outcome: A single scrolling row works; the scroll fades rely on scroll-driven animations (Newly) and `hidden=until-found` is Limited (official claim)
mwg:tabs:3.story: When there are too many tabs, wrapping feels natural, but the selected tab may end up on the second row and the visual "you are here" disappears. The guide offers three strategies, each with its own fallback.
mwg:tabs:3.unlock: Edge fades on a scroll container follow the scroll position and vanish at the end, in pure CSS. Rows with many tabs or tags can stay on one line without getting lost.
mwg:tabs:3.support: Scroll-driven animations: Newly (2026-10-27); hidden="until-found": Limited; interpolate-size: Limited

mwg:toolbar.title: Disable with aria-disabled so controls stay focusable
mwg:toolbar.action: Mark temporarily unavailable toolbar buttons with `aria-disabled="true"` and ignore clicks
mwg:toolbar.blocker: With `disabled`, the button cannot be focused and arrow-key movement skips it, so users don't know it exists (quote: "Disable with `aria-disabled=\"true\"` rather than `disabled` so the control stays focusable and reachable by arrow keys.")
mwg:toolbar.outcome: The button stays focusable and its state can be read out (official claim)
mwg:toolbar.story: Same opponent group as copy-button: the way something is disabled or hidden locks keyboard users out. In a toolbar, with one Tab stop and arrow keys stepping through, a skipped button effectively does not exist.

mwg:toolbar:2.title: Give the toolbar a single Tab stop with focusgroup
mwg:toolbar:2.action: Add `focusgroup="toolbar wrap"` to the `role="toolbar"` container and let the browser handle arrow keys and the roving tab stop
mwg:toolbar:2.blocker: (missing) The guide requires "only one item in the tab order at a time" but does not describe what concretely happens when every button is a Tab stop (quote: "MANDATORY: Only one item is in the tab order at a time.")
mwg:toolbar:2.story: Same shape as the tabs focusgroup line: a new attribute replaces hand-written focus management, but the opponent is stated only as a rule.
mwg:toolbar:2.unlock: Like focusgroup for tabs: the whole toolbar is one Tab stop with arrow-key movement handled by the browser. Keyboard support for editor-style tools comes almost for free.
mwg:toolbar:2.support: focusgroup: Limited (Chrome/Edge 150); Anchor positioning core properties: Newly (the Limited stated in the guide is the group status; see app-menus)

mwg:form-factor-adaptation.title: Lay out components with container queries, not viewport width
mwg:form-factor-adaptation.action: Use container queries for component layout; keep media queries for the input device and user settings
mwg:form-factor-adaptation.blocker: Laying out components with viewport-width media queries means a component cannot adapt when placed in a sidebar or narrow column (quote: "Use container queries instead of viewport-width media queries for component layout, so a component adapts wherever it is placed.")
mwg:form-factor-adaptation.outcome: Container queries are Widely available; components adapt to the container they are in (official claim)
mwg:form-factor-adaptation.story: The same card in the main column and in a sidebar sees the same viewport width but very different available width. The guide also warns that querying height on an `inline-size` container does nothing ("it measures only width").

mwg:form-factor-adaptation:2.title: Nothing clipped at 320px wide
mwg:form-factor-adaptation:2.action: Use `min-block-size` instead of a fixed height on anything with text, don't truncate headings with ellipsis, and don't clip controls with `overflow: hidden` on parents
mwg:form-factor-adaptation:2.blocker: Fixed heights, truncated headings and clipping parents cut off text or buttons on narrow screens or with enlarged text (quote: "DO NOT truncate headings with `text-overflow: ellipsis`, and do not clip controls with `overflow: hidden` on their parents.")
mwg:form-factor-adaptation:2.outcome: Only mature properties are used, and content stays intact at 320 CSS px (official claim)
mwg:form-factor-adaptation:2.story: WCAG 1.4.10 requires no clipping at 320px wide. The split with single-line-overflow: labels may be truncated visually, headings may not.

mwg:natural-interactions.title: Never remove focus outlines without an equally visible replacement
mwg:natural-interactions.action: Use `:focus-visible` to show keyboard focus rings and hide them only for mouse clicks
mwg:natural-interactions.blocker: `outline: none` removes the focus ring, so keyboard users cannot see where they are (quote: "DO NOT remove focus outlines (`outline: none` or `outline: 0`) without providing an equally visible replacement with at least a 3:1 contrast ratio against the page (WCAG 1.4.11).")
mwg:natural-interactions.outcome: `:focus-visible` is Widely available: no ring on mouse click, a ring for keyboard use (official claim)
mwg:natural-interactions.story: Focus rings usually get removed so an ugly box doesn't appear after clicking. `:focus-visible` separates the two needs, so looks no longer cost keyboard users.

mwg:natural-interactions:2.title: Menus may open on hover, but never only on hover
mwg:natural-interactions:2.action: Trigger dropdowns declaratively with `<button popovertarget>` so click, tap and keyboard all open them and `Esc` closes them
mwg:natural-interactions:2.blocker: Opening menus only on hover leaves keyboard and touch users unable to open them (quote: "Menus and dropdowns may open on hover, but never only on hover: they also open on click, tap, and keyboard activation, stay open while the pointer moves onto them, and close with Esc (WCAG 2.1.1, 1.4.13).")
mwg:natural-interactions:2.outcome: Popover builds in click, keyboard and dismissal behaviour; popover is Newly and older browsers need a polyfill (official claim)
mwg:natural-interactions:2.story: Same group as the `title` line in single-line-overflow: interactions that only work with a mouse. A declarative popover lets the browser provide open and close behaviour, so you don't have to add keyboard and touch support yourself.
mwg:natural-interactions:2.unlock: Dropdowns and overlays declared with `popovertarget` get click, keyboard, Esc and click-outside behaviour, and an animation growing from the trigger needs only CSS.

mwg:expose-canvas-content-to-browser-fea.title: Draw real DOM into the canvas so its content is no longer invisible to the browser
mwg:expose-canvas-content-to-browser-fea.action: Put real HTML children (marked `drawable`) inside `<canvas content="drawable">` and draw them in `onpaint` with `drawElementImage()` (or copy them to a texture in WebGL/WebGPU)
mwg:expose-canvas-content-to-browser-fea.blocker: Content drawn on a regular `<canvas>` is invisible to screen readers, indexing, translation tools, find-in-page and print (quote: "Regular `<canvas>` content is not exposed to browser features such as screen readers, indexing, translation tools, accessibility assistive tools, find-in-page, print, etc.")
mwg:expose-canvas-content-to-browser-fea.outcome: The content stays in the DOM so browser features keep working, but only Chrome 157+ supports it; elsewhere you overlay HTML on the canvas with CSS or use the `three-html-render` polyfill (official claim)
mwg:expose-canvas-content-to-browser-fea.story: A canvas has always been an opaque block of pixels: text on it cannot be selected, searched or translated, and assistive tech cannot read it. The new API keeps the canvas's children laid out and in the DOM tree while the canvas only decides how to paint them; in 2D the browser even aligns hit testing automatically. Cross-origin content cannot be drawn, and with Chrome-only support you have to maintain the fallback alongside it to cover other browsers.
mwg:expose-canvas-content-to-browser-fea.unlock: Text drawn on a canvas (charts, whiteboards, map labels) can be found with Ctrl+F, translated and read by screen readers without maintaining a hidden DOM copy. Chrome 157+ only for now.
mwg:expose-canvas-content-to-browser-fea.support: HTML-in-Canvas: Limited (Chrome 157+, stable since 2026-11-03; not Firefox or Safari). The guide's fallback section still says "HTML-in-canvas is not natively supported by any major browser yet.", which is out of date

mwg:export-html-media-from-canvas.title: Let the browser paint HTML into the canvas and export it, instead of a library redrawing the DOM
mwg:export-html-media-from-canvas.action: Put the HTML to export inside `<canvas content="drawable">`, draw it with `drawElementImage()`, then export an image or video with `toDataURL()`, `toBlob()` or `captureStream()`
mwg:export-html-media-from-canvas.blocker: The old approach relies on bulky third-party libraries that parse DOM nodes and CSS properties one by one to rebuild a facsimile on a canvas: expensive, error-prone and often missing modern CSS layout features (quote: "This approach is computationally expensive, error-prone, and frequently fails to support modern CSS layout features.")
mwg:export-html-media-from-canvas.outcome: The browser's own rendering engine paints it, so the export matches the screen; but only Chrome 157+ supports it, and elsewhere the fallback is exactly `html2canvas`, `dom-to-image` or `snapdom` (`rrweb` for frame-by-frame capture), or a warning that export is unsupported (official claim)
mwg:export-html-media-from-canvas.story: Saving a piece of the page as an image has meant a library re-implementing the browser's layout and painting in JS, and getting it wrong whenever a new CSS feature shows up. The new API has the real engine paint the HTML subtree into a canvas, after which the existing canvas export methods work. Outside Chrome, the fallback is those same libraries, so the opponent stands untouched.
mwg:export-html-media-from-canvas.unlock: Dashboards, styled documents and interactive charts can be saved as a PNG identical to the screen, or an HTML interaction can be recorded as video with `captureStream()`, without loading a screenshot library. Chrome 157+ only for now.
mwg:export-html-media-from-canvas.support: HTML-in-Canvas: Limited (Chrome 157+, stable since 2026-11-03; not Firefox or Safari). The guide's fallback section still says "HTML-in-canvas is not natively supported by any major browser yet.", which is out of date

mwg:interactive-content-in-3d-scenes.title: Project real DOM into a 3D scene and hand interaction back to the browser
mwg:interactive-content-in-3d-scenes.action: Copy `drawable` HTML elements into a texture (WebGL `texElementSubImage2D()`, WebGPU `drawElementImageToTexture()`, Three.js `HTMLTexture`), then align each element with the 3D image using `canvas.updateElementGeometry()`
mwg:interactive-content-in-3d-scenes.blocker: (missing) The guide only says complex raycasting or custom event handling is no longer required, without saying where the hand-written version fails (quote: "they retain full interactivity—allowing users to click buttons, select text, and trigger focus states natively without requiring complex raycasting or custom event handling")
mwg:interactive-content-in-3d-scenes.outcome: Elements stay in the DOM layout tree, so clicks, text selection and focus states are handled by the browser; but only Chrome 157+ supports it, and elsewhere the fallback is overlaying HTML on the canvas with CSS or the `three-html-render` polyfill (official claim)
mwg:interactive-content-in-3d-scenes.story: A panel in a 3D scene used to be a texture: clicks had to be converted with raycasting and events dispatched by hand. With the new API a real element sits behind the texture, and the developer only converts the MVP matrix into a `canvasTransform` each frame to tell the browser where it was drawn. The opponent is described only as "complex": effort, not an observable failure. Matrix syncing is still manual, though Three.js's `InteractionManager` does it for you.
mwg:interactive-content-in-3d-scenes.unlock: Screens, boards and control panels inside a 3D scene can be real forms and buttons that accept typing, selection and keyboard focus, with no raycasting-to-event code. Good for product showcases or property panels in a 3D editor. Chrome 157+ only for now.
mwg:interactive-content-in-3d-scenes.support: HTML-in-Canvas: Limited (Chrome 157+, stable since 2026-11-03; not Firefox or Safari). The guide's fallback section still says "HTML-in-canvas is not natively supported by any major browser yet.", which is out of date

mwg:apply-webgl-shaders.title: Apply shaders directly to interactive HTML
mwg:apply-webgl-shaders.action: Upload `drawable` HTML elements as a WebGL texture with `texElementSubImage2D()`, apply fragment/vertex shaders, then align hit testing with the drawn pixels using `canvas.updateElementGeometry()`
mwg:apply-webgl-shaders.blocker: (missing) The guide only says native accessibility, text selection and DOM events are retained after applying shaders, without saying what the previous approach was or where it broke (quote: "This enables applying high-performance fragment and vertex shaders natively to fully interactive UI components, such as buttons, input fields, and rich text, while retaining native accessibility, text selection, and DOM event handling.")
mwg:apply-webgl-shaders.outcome: The guide claims buttons, inputs and rich text stay interactive under a shader; but only Chrome 157+ supports it, and elsewhere the fallback is overlaying HTML on the canvas with CSS (so no shader effect) or the `three-html-render` polyfill (official claim)
mwg:apply-webgl-shaders.story: Effects like ripple distortion, lighting and color grading only work on textures, and a texture is not an element. The new API turns a real element's painted output into a texture while the element itself stays in the DOM to receive input. The guide never describes the old approach, so the opponent is marked missing. You still have to allocate the texture with `texImage2D()`, reallocate only on size change, and handle `captureElementImage()` throwing before the first paint.
mwg:apply-webgl-shaders.unlock: A real button that ripples when pressed, or a real input with glass refraction or CRT scanlines: the effect is a GPU shader, yet you can still type, select text and reach it with a screen reader. Chrome 157+ only for now.
mwg:apply-webgl-shaders.support: HTML-in-Canvas: Limited (Chrome 157+, stable since 2026-11-03; not Firefox or Safari). The guide's fallback section still says "HTML-in-canvas is not natively supported by any major browser yet.", which is out of date

mwg:accessibility.title: One h1 per page so screen readers can find the main heading
mwg:accessibility.action: Use a single `<h1>` for the page's main heading and `<h2>`–`<h6>` for the rest (a dialog's main heading is the exception)
mwg:accessibility.blocker: With several `<h1>` elements on a page, screen reader users can't tell which one is the main heading (quote: "Having more than one `<h1>` element on a page makes it difficult for screen reader users to identify the actual main heading.")
mwg:accessibility.outcome: Keeping one `<h1>` removes the ambiguity; this is a pure markup rule and the guide gives no support data (official claim)
mwg:accessibility.story: Screen reader users often jump to the h1 or scan the heading list to orient themselves, and multiple h1s break that entry point. The guide exempts h1s inside `<dialog>` / `role="dialog"`, because a dialog is a separate window.
mwg:accessibility.support: N/A (the guide has no browser support data at all)

mwg:accessibility:2.title: When a heading must toggle content, don't put it inside summary
mwg:accessibility:2.action: When a heading also acts as a disclosure trigger, use an ARIA accordion/disclosure where the heading wraps a button, not `<details>`/`<summary>`
mwg:accessibility:2.blocker: Some browsers expose `<summary>` as a button and strip all roles from its children, so the heading inside disappears (quote: "Some browsers still expose this element as a button, which removes all roles from its children including headings.")
mwg:accessibility:2.outcome: With the heading wrapping the button, the heading stays in the accessibility tree (official claim)
mwg:accessibility:2.story: Same opponent as in the accordion and navbar guides: the `summary` role is implemented inconsistently. This general guide doesn't name a screen reader, only "some browsers".
mwg:accessibility:2.support: N/A (the guide has no browser support data at all)

mwg:accessibility:3.title: Use list markup only for real lists
mwg:accessibility:3.action: Use `<ul>`/`<ol>` only for repeated, contiguous items; don't wrap paragraphs in a list
mwg:accessibility:3.blocker: Marking separate paragraphs as a list makes screen readers announce list information, so users hear confusing and redundant content (quote: "screen readers will announce list information when they encounter lists, therefore leading to a screen reader hearing potentially confusing and redundant information about the related content.")
mwg:accessibility:3.outcome: Content that isn't a list is no longer read out as one (official claim)
mwg:accessibility:3.story: List markup makes a screen reader say "list, N items" first, so misused lists become noise. The same section notes that checkboxes and radio buttons already announce their count, so wrapping them in a list duplicates it.
mwg:accessibility:3.support: N/A (the guide has no browser support data at all)

mwg:accessible-error-announcement.title: Sync aria-invalid with :user-invalid so errors aren't announced before input
mwg:accessible-error-announcement.action: Show errors with `:user-invalid`, and use a small script on `blur`/`change`/`input`/`invalid` to check it and set `aria-invalid` to match; until then, set `aria-invalid="false"` explicitly
mwg:accessible-error-announcement.blocker: With `:invalid` alone, a screen reader says "Invalid entry" as soon as the user tabs into an empty required field, before any interaction (quote: "screen readers might announce \"Invalid entry\" the moment a user tabs into a required field that is currently empty.")
mwg:accessible-error-announcement.outcome: `:user-invalid` is Widely available, and the programmatic state now appears at the same moment as the visual state (official claim)
mwg:accessible-error-announcement.story: `:user-invalid` only affects the visuals; it doesn't touch ARIA. The guide also points out that Firefox and Safari expose an empty required field as invalid from page load, so `aria-invalid` can't be left unset and must be `false`. You still write the bridging script yourself, because there is no "UserInvalidChanged" event.

mwg:accessible-error-announcement:2.title: Reference the error from aria-describedby only while it's shown
mwg:accessible-error-announcement:2.action: Point the field at its error message with `data-error`, and let the script add that id to `aria-describedby` only while the field is invalid
mwg:accessible-error-announcement:2.blocker: Referencing the error from `aria-describedby` in the markup means it is read even while hidden, so users hear the error before interacting (quote: "text that `aria-describedby` references is announced even when it's hidden, so the error would be read out before the user has interacted.")
mwg:accessible-error-announcement:2.outcome: The error message is referenced only while it is visible (official claim)
mwg:accessible-error-announcement:2.story: The error element is always in the page, just hidden with `display: none`, so leaving the reference in place feels harmless. But `aria-describedby` ignores visibility, so the reference itself has to follow the state.
mwg:accessible-error-announcement:2.support: :user-valid / :user-invalid: Widely (2023-11-02); no support data given for aria-describedby

mwg:accessible-error-announcement:3.title: Announce errors through one shared polite live region, not a live region per error
mwg:accessible-error-announcement:3.action: Put one `aria-live="polite"` region on the page and write "label: error" into it about 500ms after a field is left or changed; after a failed submit, move focus to the first invalid field
mwg:accessible-error-announcement:3.blocker: Making each error message its own live region fails because it is shown rather than changed, so screen readers don't announce it reliably (quote: "a live region that is shown, rather than changed, isn't announced reliably.")
mwg:accessible-error-announcement:3.outcome: The shared region announces by changing its content, and the delay keeps it from talking over the next field (official claim)
mwg:accessible-error-announcement:3.story: A common pattern is putting `aria-live` on each error `<span>` and toggling its display, which announces only some of the time. The guide uses a single announcer that receives text instead. When the field is fixed, the announcer is also cleared so the old error isn't found later while reading the page.
mwg:accessible-error-announcement:3.support: :user-valid / :user-invalid: Widely (2023-11-02); no support data given for live regions

mwg:accessible-generated-content.title: Silence decorative glyphs with content's alt-text argument
mwg:accessible-generated-content.action: Add alt text to `content` after a `/`: `content: " →" / "";` for decoration, `content: url(icon.svg) / "Save";` for a meaningful icon
mwg:accessible-generated-content.blocker: Without the `/` syntax, decorative glyphs inserted with `::after` are read out by screen readers (quote: "Fallback: render the glyph in browsers without `/` support (screen readers there will still announce it)")
mwg:accessible-generated-content.outcome: The alt-text syntax is Newly available (2024-07-09); older browsers need a preceding `content` line without `/` as a fallback, where the glyph is still announced and non-empty alt text is lost (official claim)
mwg:accessible-generated-content.story: CSS-added arrows and separator dots turn into noise like "right arrow" in a screen reader. The new syntax lets CSS itself declare "don't read this" or "read it as this". The guide stresses this is harm reduction: meaningful text still belongs in the DOM.
mwg:accessible-generated-content.unlock: Arrows, separators and status icons inserted with CSS can be declared silent, or given a spoken label, right in the stylesheet, without wrapping each icon in an extra `aria-hidden` span. An icon system can live entirely in CSS without adding screen reader noise.
mwg:accessible-generated-content.support: Alt text for generated content: Newly (2024-07-09; Chrome 77, Edge 79, Firefox 128, Safari 17.4)

mwg:accessible-generated-content:2.title: Don't repeat text already in the DOM as content alt text
mwg:accessible-generated-content:2.action: Use the alt-text argument only when the text differs from the primary value and isn't already in the DOM
mwg:accessible-generated-content:2.blocker: A button labelled "Save" with `/ "Save"` on its `::before` icon is read as "Save save" (quote: "A screen reader would read it out as \"Save save\".")
mwg:accessible-generated-content:2.outcome: Not naming the icon again means no duplicate announcement (official claim)
mwg:accessible-generated-content:2.story: The new syntax invites the idea that every icon needs alt text, which then stacks on top of the button's own label. The guide also says images are presentational by default, so don't add empty alt text, and emoji alt text is only for when it differs from the official name.
mwg:accessible-generated-content:2.support: Alt text for generated content: Newly (2024-07-09)

mwg:respect-os-text-scale.title: Use meta text-scale so the page follows the system font size
mwg:respect-os-text-scale.action: Put `<meta name="text-scale" content="scale">` in `<head>`, size text and spacing in `rem`/`em`, and use unitless line heights
mwg:respect-os-text-scale.blocker: Users set a larger system font size on iOS/Android, but mobile browsers ignore it by default and the page text stays the same (quote: "By default, mobile browsers ignore these OS-level accessibility settings to prevent legacy, fixed-pixel websites from breaking visually.")
mwg:respect-os-text-scale.outcome: Only Chrome/Edge 146 support it; Firefox and Safari keep the default size, leaving users with manual zoom or pinch-to-zoom (official claim)
mwg:respect-os-text-scale.story: Browsers ignore the system font size to protect old fixed-px sites. The meta tag is the page declaring "my layout can take it", and only then is the system scale applied to `1rem`. After opting in you must not set `font-size` on `:root` yourself, nor multiply by `env(preferred-text-scale)` again, or scaling is blocked or doubled.
mwg:respect-os-text-scale.unlock: Web pages can follow the phone's system font size (Dynamic Type) like native apps, so older or low-vision users don't have to adjust every site. Reading and documentation pages benefit most; Chrome/Edge 146+ only for now.
mwg:respect-os-text-scale.support: <meta name="text-scale">: Limited (Chrome 146, Edge 146; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:respect-os-text-scale:2.title: Fluid font sizes need a rem component, not vw alone
mwg:respect-os-text-scale:2.action: Write fluid font sizes like `clamp(2rem, 1.25rem + 2vw, 4rem)` so they have both a font-relative and a viewport-relative part
mwg:respect-os-text-scale:2.blocker: With `font-size: 5vw` alone, text doesn't fully respond to the user's text scaling (quote: "The font size does not respond fully to user text scaling")
mwg:respect-os-text-scale:2.outcome: With a `rem` component, both the system font size and browser zoom affect the text size (official claim)
mwg:respect-os-text-scale:2.story: Pure vw sizes follow only the viewport width, so when the user enlarges text the headings don't move. The guide adds rules of thumb: keep the maximum no more than 2.5 times the minimum, and test 200% text resize and reflow at 320 CSS px wide.
mwg:respect-os-text-scale:2.support: — (the guide gives support data only for meta text-scale, not for `clamp()`/`rem`)

mwg:respect-os-text-scale:3.title: With text-scale on, don't hard-code font-size on html
mwg:respect-os-text-scale:3.action: Leave the root font size to the browser: no `font-size` on `:root`/`html`, whether absolute, relative or calculated
mwg:respect-os-text-scale:3.blocker: Writing `font-size: 16px` on `html` can stop the browser from applying text scaling (quote: "This can prevent the browser from applying text scaling")
mwg:respect-os-text-scale:3.outcome: Leaving the root size to the browser lets the system scale apply, but that only matters in Chrome/Edge 146+, which support meta text-scale (official claim)
mwg:respect-os-text-scale:3.story: Many resets and design systems pin 16px on `html` as a baseline, and that one line cancels the opt-in. The guide lists it as a DO NOT, and separately warns against combining it with `env(preferred-text-scale)`, which scales twice.

mwg:language-detection.title: Detect text language in the browser with LanguageDetector
mwg:language-detection.action: Check with `LanguageDetector.availability()`, create the detector from a user gesture with `LanguageDetector.create()`, and get a confidence-ranked language list from `detect()`
mwg:language-detection.blocker: (missing) The guide only says it reduces the need for heavy external libraries or costly server calls, without saying where the old approach fails (quote: "it enhances user privacy and reduces the need for heavy external libraries or costly server-side calls.")
mwg:language-detection.outcome: Only Chrome 138 and Edge 148 support it; elsewhere you fall back to a server or cloud API, or disable detection (official claim)
mwg:language-detection.story: Uses include detecting the source language before translation and setting the right `lang` on content. The guide stresses detection runs locally and sends nothing to Google or third parties, but never describes a concrete failure of the old way. The model download needs a user gesture, 22 GB of storage and 16 GB of RAM, and accuracy drops sharply on very short phrases.
mwg:language-detection.unlock: Pasted text can have its language detected on-device and get the right `lang` automatically on comments or note paragraphs, so screen readers pronounce it correctly, without sending the content to a server. Chrome/Edge desktop only for now, with hardware requirements.
mwg:language-detection.support: Language detector: Limited (Chrome 138, Edge 148; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:language-model.title: Run Gemini Nano in the browser with the Prompt API
mwg:language-model.action: Check with `LanguageModel.availability()`, download the model from a user gesture via `LanguageModel.create()`, then handle text, image and audio input with `prompt()`/`promptStreaming()`
mwg:language-model.blocker: (missing) The guide only lists the benefits of running locally (privacy, lower server cost, offline), without saying where the old approach fails (quote: "This built-in AI approach ensures user privacy, reduces server costs, and enables offline functionality.")
mwg:language-model.outcome: Only Chrome 148 supports it; Edge, Firefox and Safari fall back to a server/cloud API or a local endpoint such as Transformers.js (official claim)
mwg:language-model.story: The guide covers session management (`clone()`, `initialPrompts`, `destroy()`), multimodal input and JSON Schema structured output. The opponent appears only as the flip side of the benefits, with no observable failure. Hardware requirements are high (22 GB storage, 16 GB RAM), and the download needs a user gesture plus visible progress.
mwg:language-model.unlock: Classify, rewrite or answer questions about images inside the page without a server, for example a notes app tagging each diary entry on-device or turning screenshots into text. Data stays on the device and it works offline. Chrome 148 desktop only for now, with hardware requirements.
mwg:language-model.support: LanguageModel: Limited (Chrome 148; not Edge, Firefox or Safari)

mwg:language-model:2.title: Always write model output with textContent, never innerHTML
mwg:language-model:2.action: Write model responses into `textContent`; when limited HTML is needed, run the Sanitizer API or DOMPurify over the **complete** output
mwg:language-model:2.blocker: Model output is untrusted and can contain injected markup, so setting `innerHTML` directly becomes XSS (quote: "Model output is untrusted and can contain injected markup. Always use `textContent` or a sanitizer.")
mwg:language-model:2.outcome: Written as plain text, it is never parsed as markup (official claim)
mwg:language-model:2.story: The usual streaming pattern is `innerHTML +=` for each chunk. The guide says that is slow and injectable, and malicious code can be split across two chunks, so sanitize the combined output, not each chunk.

mwg:language-model:3.title: Set aria-busy while streaming so screen readers read the full response, not each chunk
mwg:language-model:3.action: Make the output container a polite live region present from page load, set `aria-busy="true"` while streaming and `false` after; don't move focus during streaming
mwg:language-model:3.blocker: Without `aria-busy`, the live region reads out every streamed chunk (quote: "so assistive technologies announce the complete response rather than each chunk")
mwg:language-model:3.outcome: Assistive tech waits until streaming ends and announces the complete response (official claim)
mwg:language-model:3.story: The typewriter effect is feedback for sighted users and broken fragments for screen reader users. When the output language differs from the page, the output element must also get `lang` so it is pronounced correctly.
mwg:language-model:3.support: — (no support data given for aria-busy / live regions)

mwg:prompt-api.title: Run Gemini Nano in the browser with the Prompt API
mwg:prompt-api.action: Check with `LanguageModel.availability()`, download the model from a user gesture via `LanguageModel.create()`, then handle text, image and audio input with `prompt()`/`promptStreaming()`
mwg:prompt-api.blocker: (missing) The guide only lists the benefits of running locally (privacy, lower server cost, offline), without saying where the old approach fails (quote: "This built-in AI approach ensures user privacy, reduces server costs, and enables offline functionality.")
mwg:prompt-api.outcome: Only Chrome 148 supports it; Edge, Firefox and Safari fall back to a server/cloud API or a local endpoint such as Transformers.js (official claim)
mwg:prompt-api.story: This guide is word-for-word identical to the language-model guide in v1.0.0. It covers session management, multimodal input and structured output; the opponent appears only as the flip side of the benefits. Hardware requirements are high, and the download needs a user gesture plus visible progress.
mwg:prompt-api.unlock: Same as `mwg:language-model`: classify, rewrite or answer questions about images inside the page without a server; data stays on the device. Chrome 148 desktop only for now.
mwg:prompt-api.support: LanguageModel: Limited (Chrome 148; not Edge, Firefox or Safari)

mwg:prompt-api:2.title: Always write model output with textContent, never innerHTML
mwg:prompt-api:2.action: Write model responses into `textContent`; when limited HTML is needed, run the Sanitizer API or DOMPurify over the **complete** output
mwg:prompt-api:2.blocker: Model output is untrusted and can contain injected markup, so setting `innerHTML` directly becomes XSS (quote: "Model output is untrusted and can contain injected markup. Always use `textContent` or a sanitizer.")
mwg:prompt-api:2.outcome: Written as plain text, it is never parsed as markup (official claim)
mwg:prompt-api:2.story: The usual streaming pattern is `innerHTML +=` for each chunk. The guide says that is slow and injectable, and malicious code can be split across two chunks, so sanitize the combined output, not each chunk.

mwg:prompt-api:3.title: Set aria-busy while streaming so screen readers read the full response, not each chunk
mwg:prompt-api:3.action: Make the output container a polite live region present from page load, set `aria-busy="true"` while streaming and `false` after; don't move focus during streaming
mwg:prompt-api:3.blocker: Without `aria-busy`, the live region reads out every streamed chunk (quote: "so assistive technologies announce the complete response rather than each chunk")
mwg:prompt-api:3.outcome: Assistive tech waits until streaming ends and announces the complete response (official claim)
mwg:prompt-api:3.story: The typewriter effect is feedback for sighted users and broken fragments for screen reader users. When the output language differs from the page, the output element must also get `lang` so it is pronounced correctly.
mwg:prompt-api:3.support: — (no support data given for aria-busy / live regions)

mwg:summarizer.title: Summarize on-device with Summarizer instead of sending articles to the cloud
mwg:summarizer.action: Call `Summarizer.availability()` and `Summarizer.create()` with the same options (type: key-points/tldr/teaser/headline) and summarize long text with `summarize()` or `summarizeStreaming()`
mwg:summarizer.blocker: When a remote service does the work, requests go to the cloud, the on-device privacy guarantee is gone, and server-side API costs are incurred (quote: "This completely nullifies the on-device privacy guarantees of the native Built-in AI APIs and will incur server-side API usage costs.")
mwg:summarizer.outcome: Only Chrome 138 and Edge 138 support it; elsewhere the fallback is exactly a remote API or a cloud-proxying polyfill, so the opponent stands untouched (official claim)
mwg:summarizer.story: The guide says summarization runs entirely on the device and nothing goes to Google. The opponent shows up in the fallback section's warning that polyfills may forward requests to cloud models. So in Firefox and Safari you either pay and hand over the data, or disable the summarize button.
mwg:summarizer.unlock: Private documents (diaries, meeting notes, email) can get a TL;DR or key points right in the page without the content leaving the device or running up an API bill, for example a "this week in three sentences" block at the top of a long weekly note. Chrome/Edge 138 desktop only for now.
mwg:summarizer.support: Summarizer: Limited (Chrome 138, Edge 138; not Firefox or Safari)

mwg:translator.title: Translate on-device with Translator instead of sending text to the cloud
mwg:translator.action: Call `Translator.availability()` and `Translator.create()` with the same `sourceLanguage`/`targetLanguage`, download the language pack from a user gesture, and translate with `translate()` or `translateStreaming()`
mwg:translator.blocker: When a remote service does the work, the on-device privacy guarantee is gone and server-side API costs often follow (quote: "Remote processing completely nullifies the on-device privacy guarantees of the native Built-in AI APIs and will often incur server-side API usage costs.")
mwg:translator.outcome: Only Chrome 138 and Edge 148 desktop support it, not mobile, Firefox or Safari; the fallback is a cloud translation API or a polyfill, so the opponent remains (official claim)
mwg:translator.story: The guide targets ephemeral content such as chat messages and user input, text not worth sending to the cloud. After the model downloads, translation needs no network. Language packs download per language pair, and `availability()` reports available, downloadable, downloading or unavailable; unavailable means taking the fallback.
mwg:translator.unlock: Chat rooms and comment sections can translate each message in place, without a third-party translation service or per-character billing; paired with language detection, users wouldn't even need to pick the source language. Chrome/Edge desktop only for now.
mwg:translator.support: Translator: Limited (Chrome 138, Edge 148; not Firefox or Safari; desktop only)

mwg:animate-to-intrinsic-sizes.title: Let height: auto transition with interpolate-size
mwg:animate-to-intrinsic-sizes.action: Set `interpolate-size: allow-keywords` on `:root` so `block-size` can transition from a fixed length to keywords like `auto`/`max-content`; use `calc-size()` when you need math on the intrinsic size
mwg:animate-to-intrinsic-sizes.blocker: In browsers without support, the size jumps straight to the target value with no transition (quote: "Browsers that do not support them will perform an instant jump to the target size.")
mwg:animate-to-intrinsic-sizes.outcome: `interpolate-size` and `calc-size()` are only in Chrome/Edge 129; Firefox and Safari still jump instantly, which the guide calls functional but less polished (official claim)
mwg:animate-to-intrinsic-sizes.story: A "show more" section or a dismissible alert growing from 0 to its content height used to need JS measuring or `max-height` hacks. The new property lets the browser interpolate, but both ends can't be keywords; one must be a length or percentage. The guide also requires setting `hidden` after collapsing to 0 and respecting `prefers-reduced-motion`.
mwg:animate-to-intrinsic-sizes.unlock: Any block whose height follows its content (notifications, expandable notes, collapsible sidebars) can expand and collapse smoothly with one line of CSS and no JS measuring. Good for dashboard cards with lots of dynamic content; Chromium only for now.
mwg:animate-to-intrinsic-sizes.support: interpolate-size: Limited (Chrome 129, Edge 129); calc-size(): Limited (Chrome 129, Edge 129); not Firefox or Safari

mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes.title: Add to, clamp and animate content sizes with calc-size()
mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes.action: Use `calc-size(<basis>, <calculation>)` on `auto`/`min-content`/`fit-content` (e.g. `calc-size(auto, size + 2rem)`, `calc-size(fit-content, min(size + …, …))`), with a plain keyword on the line before as fallback
mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes.blocker: Browsers can't interpolate between a length and an intrinsic sizing keyword by default, e.g. `0px` to `auto` (quote: "By default, browsers cannot interpolate between a length (e.g., `0px`) and an intrinsic keyword (e.g., `auto`).")
mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes.outcome: `calc-size()` is only in Chrome/Edge 129; other browsers drop the whole declaration and the animation becomes an instant jump (official claim)
mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes.story: "Content width plus 2rem" or "content height but capped" used to need JS measuring. `calc-size()` turns intrinsic sizes into values you can compute and interpolate. The guide draws a clear line: for a plain `0` to `auto` animation use `interpolate-size`, use `calc-size()` only for math; it also warns that percentages inside resolve against the container, not `size`.
mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes.unlock: Labels, buttons and floating panels that are "as wide as their content plus some breathing room, up to a cap" can be written in pure CSS and grow smoothly when expanded, for example a button that stretches from an icon to icon plus text on hover. Chromium only for now.
mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes.support: calc-size(): Limited (Chrome 129, Edge 129); interpolate-size: Limited (Chrome 129, Edge 129)

mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes:2.title: Set visibility: hidden when collapsing to zero height
mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes:2.action: Set `visibility: hidden` on the collapsed state and `visible` on the open state, and include `visibility` in the transition so content stays visible until it finishes closing
mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes:2.blocker: Collapsing only `block-size` to 0 hides content visually, but screen readers still read it and its links and controls stay in the tab order (quote: "Collapsing to zero size (`block-size: 0` or `height: 0`) hides content only visually: screen readers still read it, and its links and controls stay in the tab order.")
mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes:2.outcome: `visibility: hidden` removes collapsed content from the accessibility tree and the tab order (official claim)
mwg:calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes:2.story: The height animation looks great, yet keyboard users tab into an invisible panel. Transitioning `visibility` too keeps both the collapse animation and the correct accessibility state.

mwg:atrule-support-conditionals.title: Detect at-rules in CSS with @supports at-rule()
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals.action: Wrap rules or declarations that only make sense when an at-rule works in `@supports at-rule(@property) { … }` (it can be nested inside a selector)
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals.blocker: (missing) The guide only says that without `at-rule()` you detect via properties/selectors, a registered-property trick, and JS as a last resort, without saying where those approaches fail (quote: "When `at-rule()` is not an option, either due to browser support or because deeper detection is needed, you can use the guidance below.")
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals.outcome: `at-rule()` is only in Chrome/Edge 148 and Firefox 157, not Safari; the guide advises using it only for at-rules that shipped later than it did (official claim)
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals.story: Knowing whether `@property` or `@function` works used to require detours, or a JS check for `CSSFunctionRule` followed by adding a class. The new syntax lets CSS branch directly. It detects by **name** only, not preludes or descriptors, and shouldn't wrap the detected at-rule by itself, since unknown rules are ignored anyway.
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals.unlock: Animations and themes that depend on `@property` or custom functions can carry their own "if unsupported, use the flat version" branch in the stylesheet instead of detecting in JS and toggling a class, so component libraries can keep progressive enhancement entirely in CSS. Not in Safari yet.
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals.support: at-rule(): Limited (Chrome 148, Edge 148, Firefox 157; not Safari)

mwg:atrule-support-conditionals:2.title: Detect style query support with an always-true query
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals:2.action: Wrap rules that should apply only when style queries work in `@container style(--a: 1) or (not (style(--a: 1))) { … }`
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals:2.blocker: Detecting style queries with `@supports at-rule(@container style(--a: 1))` or `@supports (container-type: style)` never matches (quote: "IMPORTANT: Do NOT try `@supports (container-type: style)` to detect support for style queries, as this will not work.")
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals:2.outcome: The always-true query always matches where style queries are supported; container style queries are Newly available (2026-05-19) (official claim)
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals:2.story: Every other container query type can be detected through a `container-type` value, but style queries have none, so the intuitive version fails silently. The guide's always-true query works with any property name, as long as both halves match.
mwg:atrule-support-conditionals:2.support: Container style queries: Newly (2026-05-19; data from the upstream design-token-reactivity guide, not given in this one)

mwg:child-state-based-styling.title: Let containers react to child state with :has() instead of JS-toggled classes
mwg:child-state-based-styling.action: Use `:has()` on the container with state pseudo-classes (`:checked`, `:invalid`, `:focus`…), e.g. `.theme-card:has(.theme-toggle:checked)` overriding the container's custom properties
mwg:child-state-based-styling.blocker: (missing) The guide only says JS no longer needs to toggle modifier classes like `.is-active` or `.has-error` on parents, without saying where hand-toggling fails (quote: "without needing JavaScript to toggle \"modifier\" classes (like `.is-active` or `.has-error`) on parent elements.")
mwg:child-state-based-styling.outcome: `:has()` is Widely available; the container's style follows the child's state directly (official claim)
mwg:child-state-based-styling.story: CSS selectors used to go only downward, so a parent reacting to a child meant event listeners adding classes. `:has()` makes a form group highlighting errors or a card lifting when a child link is focused pure CSS. The guide advises scoping `:has()` to the nearest component container, not `body`, to avoid wide recalculations.

mwg:content-based-styling.title: Switch layouts with :has() based on whether a child exists
mwg:content-based-styling.action: Use `:has(img)` on the component container to switch to a side-by-side layout, and `:not(:has(img))` for the no-image style
mwg:content-based-styling.blocker: (missing) The guide only says JS or template conditionals used to inject modifier classes like `.card--has-image`, without saying where that fails (quote: "Historically, applying different layouts to a component based on its content required either JavaScript or conditional logic in your HTML templating language to inject modifier classes")
mwg:content-based-styling.outcome: `:has()` is Widely available; the layout follows the actual DOM content (official claim)
mwg:content-based-styling.story: One card component needs two layouts, with and without an image, which used to mean the HTML-generating side knew the content and added a class. `:has()` lets the stylesheet look at the content itself. For a fallback, the guide prefers a server-side template class, since content is known at render time.

mwg:css-layout.title: Remove the replaced-element gap with display: block, not overflow: hidden
mwg:css-layout.action: Give ``, ``, `
mwg:css-layout.blocker: These replaced elements are `display: inline` by default, which adds a gap in some layouts (quote: "certain replaced elements like ``, ``, `
mwg:css-layout.outcome: With block display the gap disappears, with no clipping needed to hide it (official claim)
mwg:css-layout.story: When a few stray px appear under an image, the usual "fix" is `overflow: hidden` on the parent to clip them, which only hides the layout problem. The guide's principle is not to mask layout issues with `overflow: hidden` and to fix them at the source.

mwg:css-layout:2.title: Reserve space for media with aspect-ratio
mwg:css-layout:2.action: Set `aspect-ratio` (e.g. `16 / 9`) on media, with `inline-size: 100%; block-size: auto`
mwg:css-layout:2.blocker: Without reserved space, images and video push the content below down once they load, causing layout shift (quote: "Use `aspect-ratio` to reserve space for media and prevent layout shift before assets load.")
mwg:css-layout:2.outcome: The ratio fixes the height up front, so the layout doesn't move when assets load (official claim)
mwg:css-layout:2.story: Text jumping down mid-read happens because an image above just finished loading. Declaring the ratio tells the browser how much height to reserve before the image arrives.

mwg:css-layout:3.title: Turn on flex-wrap: wrap for rows that might not fit
mwg:css-layout:3.action: Whenever overflow is possible, set `flex-wrap: wrap` on the flex container; add `min-inline-size: 0` to items with long URLs or code
mwg:css-layout:3.blocker: `nowrap` without `overflow: auto/hidden` makes items spill out of the container on narrow viewports (quote: "`nowrap` without `overflow: auto/hidden` will spill on narrow viewports.")
mwg:css-layout:3.outcome: With wrapping, items stay inside the container (official claim)
mwg:css-layout:3.story: A row of buttons that looks fine on desktop runs off the screen on a phone. The guide also suggests layering `flex-wrap: balance` after `wrap` to even out rows and avoid a lone orphan on the last row, but that is a Limited new feature outside this line.
mwg:css-layout:3.support: — (no support data given for flex-wrap: wrap; flex-wrap: balance in the same section is Limited, Chrome 150, Edge 150)

mwg:css.title: Exclude with :not() instead of overriding with a later rule
mwg:css.action: Use `:not()` to exclude irrelevant states or targets, e.g. `li:not(:last-child)`, `button:hover:not(:disabled)`
mwg:css.blocker: Styling first and overriding with another rule breaks when the two rules swap order, so disabled buttons get a hover background; the override can also clobber a value set elsewhere (quote: "If we reorder the two rules, we will get a hover background on disabled buttons!")
mwg:css.outcome: A selector that doesn't overmatch works regardless of rule order (official claim)
mwg:css.story: "Add a border to all, then remove it from the last" is common, but it doesn't express the real intent and depends on rule order. The guide separates two cases: use `:not()` to exclude irrelevant targets; overriding for specialization (buttons are neutral, primary ones blue) is fine.
mwg:css.support: N/A (the guide has no browser support data at all)

mwg:css:2.title: Exclude nested subtrees with @scope, not :not() plus descendants
mwg:css:2.action: Use `@scope (.card) to (.content) { … }` to select elements inside the card but not inside `.content`
mwg:css:2.blocker: `.card :not(.content *)` doesn't work as expected with nested cards and excludes the wrong elements (quote: "For example, `.card :not(.content *)` will not work as expected for nested cards.")
mwg:css:2.outcome: `@scope` accounts for proximity, so nested cards work (official claim)
mwg:css:2.story: `:not()` only asks whether some ancestor matches, not which one is nearest, so it goes wrong once components nest. The lower bound of `@scope` makes exclusion follow the nearest scope root. The same guide uses `@scope` to fix `.dark .invert` / `.light .invert` always resolving to one theme when nested.
mwg:css:2.support: N/A (the guide has no browser support data at all; no external @scope data added)

mwg:css:3.title: Don't write global resets on *
mwg:css:3.action: Apply resets to specific element types or conditions, not to `*`
mwg:css:3.blocker: Resets on `*` can't be overridden by web components or lower-priority cascade layers without `!important` (quote: "they cannot be overridden by web components or lower-priority cascade layers (without `!important`).")
mwg:css:3.outcome: The guide only says to target specific elements, without stating what happens to the opponent afterwards
mwg:css:3.story: `* { box-sizing: border-box; margin: 0 }` is almost a reflex, but it hits every element, including parts of web components that want to decide for themselves. The guide advocates managing priority with `@layer` and `:where()`, which a global reset works against.
